1.name: Julia Robinson
1.link: Julia loved counting numbers and arranging objects, and today the children hop along the number strip and find the rule that makes a counting pattern.
1.story: Julia Robinson was born in 1919 in the United States. She wrote that one of her earliest memories was arranging pebbles in the shadow of a giant cactus. She also said she had always liked the counting numbers. When she grew up she became a mathematician who worked on hard number puzzles. In 1975 she became the first woman mathematician elected to the US National Academy of Sciences.
1.blurb: Julia Robinson (USA, 1919-1985) loved the counting numbers, and as a small child she liked arranging pebbles. She grew up to be a mathematician who worked on hard number puzzles.
1.q: Julia puts pebbles in rows. Row 1 has 3 pebbles, row 2 has 6, row 3 has 9. How many pebbles are in row 5? What is the rule?
1.a: 15 pebbles. The rule is add 3 each time (row 4 has 12, row 5 has 15).

2.name: Robert Recorde
2.country: Wales (born in Tenby), worked in England
2.link: Recorde's equals sign says both sides are worth the same, which is exactly what children check when they balance number bonds like 4 + 4 = 5 + 3.
2.story: Robert Recorde was a doctor from Tenby, in Wales. He also wrote maths books, as talks between a teacher and a pupil. In 1557 he used the sign = in a book. He was tired of writing the words "is equal to" again and again. He chose two straight lines of the same length, because, he said, no two things can be more equal. Today the sign tells us that both sides have the same amount.
2.blurb: Robert Recorde (Wales, about 1510-1558) was a doctor who wrote maths books. In 1557 he used the sign = for the first time in a book, because no two things can be more equal than two straight lines of the same length.
2.q: Use Recorde's sign. Fill in the missing number so that both sides are equal: 4 + 4 = 5 + __

3.name: Marie Neurath
3.country: Germany (born in Braunschweig); worked in Austria, the Netherlands and England
3.link: A picture graph uses one small picture for each thing, the same idea Marie used, so we can count the pictures and compare quickly.
3.story: Marie Neurath helped to make a way of showing numbers with pictures. It was called Isotype. In Isotype, if there is more of something, you draw more little pictures of the same size, not one bigger picture. That makes the pictures easy to count and compare. Marie was the "transformer" on the team. Her job was to turn facts and numbers into a clear picture plan.
3.blurb: Marie Neurath (Germany, 1898-1986) helped make Isotype, a way of showing numbers with little pictures. More of something means more pictures, all the same size.
3.q: Marie draws one small apple picture for each child who chose apples. 6 children chose apples and 4 chose pears. How many apple pictures does she draw? How many more apple pictures than pear pictures?

4.name: Ingrid Daubechies
4.country: Belgium (born in Houthalen); now works in the USA
4.link: Doubling is a growing pattern with a rule, and weaving is a repeating pattern, so Ingrid's childhood games are the same kind of pattern the children build today.
4.story: Ingrid Daubechies grew up in Belgium. As a girl she liked weaving, which makes patterns from threads, and she liked finding out how things work. When she could not sleep, she worked out the powers of 2 in her head: 2, 4, 8, 16 and on. She was amazed at how fast they grow. Today she is a maths professor, and her ideas help computers keep pictures in small files.
4.blurb: Ingrid Daubechies (Belgium, born 1954) liked weaving as a girl. When she could not sleep she doubled numbers in her head: 2, 4, 8, 16 and on. Now she is a maths professor.
4.q: Try Ingrid's doubling game: 1, 2, 4, 8, __, __. What is the rule? What are the next two numbers?
4.a: The rule is double each time (multiply by 2). The next two numbers are 16 and 32.

5.name: René Descartes
5.country: France (born in La Haye en Touraine)
5.link: A mystery number is an unknown number, and Descartes' habit of writing it as x is how we write these problems, then work backwards to find it.
5.story: René Descartes was born in France in 1596. In 1637 he published a book called La Géométrie. In it he used letters from the end of the alphabet, x, y and z, for numbers we do not know yet, and letters from the start, a, b and c, for numbers we do know. People still do this today. When you have a mystery number, you can call it x.
5.blurb: René Descartes (France, 1596-1650) wrote a book in 1637 that used x, y and z for numbers we do not know yet. We still call a mystery number x.
5.q: Call the mystery number x. x + 8 = 14. Work backwards: what is x?

6.name: Isaac Newton
6.link: Coins only work as money when each one is made to the right size and weight, so people can count and trade fairly.
6.story: Isaac Newton is famous for his big ideas in science. But for many years he also had a job at the Royal Mint, which is where English coins were made. He started there in 1696, when old silver coins were being worn out and replaced with new ones. The people at the Mint cared about every coin having the right weight and the right amount of metal. Newton worked there until 1727.
6.blurb: Isaac Newton (England, 1642-1727) is famous for science, but he also worked at the Royal Mint, where English coins were made. The Mint cared that every coin had the right weight.
6.q: You have one 10-cent coin and some 5-cent coins. You want 20 cents. How many 5-cent coins do you need?

7.name: Johannes Kepler
7.link: A snowflake with six corners is shaped like a hexagon, and the children count the sides and corners of shapes today.
7.story: Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer. In 1611 he wrote a small booklet about snowflakes as a New Year's gift for a friend. He noticed that snowflakes have six corners, and he asked why. He thought about the six-sided cells of honeycomb and how things pack together. He could not give a final answer, so he wrote down his ideas and left the rest for others to find out. Asking "why?" is how a shape safari begins.
7.blurb: Johannes Kepler (Germany, 1571-1630) was an astronomer. In 1611 he noticed that snowflakes have six corners and asked why.
7.q: Kepler's snowflake has six corners. What shape has 6 straight sides and 6 corners? How many sides do two of these shapes have altogether?

8.name: Leonhard Euler
8.link: Euler used circles to show how things sort into groups, which is what the children do in Logic and Sorting.
8.story: Leonhard Euler came from Switzerland. Starting in 1760 he wrote letters to a princess in Germany to explain science and ideas to her. In some letters he drew circles to show groups. A small circle inside a big circle shows a smaller group inside a bigger one. Many years later, people called these Euler's circles. Drawing groups as circles still helps us sort things and think clearly.
8.blurb: Leonhard Euler (Switzerland, 1707-1783) drew circles in his letters to show groups. A small circle inside a big circle is a smaller group inside a bigger one.
8.q: Draw a big circle for animals and a small circle inside it for cats. Is every cat an animal? Is every animal a cat?
8.a: Yes, every cat is an animal. No, not every animal is a cat (a dog is an animal but not a cat).
8.legend: Cats-and-animals is our own example, not from Euler's letters.

9.name: Al-Biruni
9.country: Khwarazm, Central Asia (in the region of today's Uzbekistan); later worked in Afghanistan and India
9.link: Al-Biruni shows that careful measuring of one length can help us find a much bigger one, and the children measure lengths with equal units and a ruler today.
9.story: Al-Biruni lived about a thousand years ago. He was born in Khwarazm, in Central Asia, and he loved to measure things. He wanted to know how big the Earth is. He measured the distance between two spots near a hill, and the angles up to the top, to find how tall the hill was. Then he climbed it and looked at the horizon. With a little maths he found a size for the Earth that is close to today's value.
9.blurb: Al-Biruni (Central Asia, 973-1048) loved to measure. He used careful measuring of a hill to work out the size of the whole Earth, and found a value close to today's.
9.q: Al-Biruni needed careful measuring. A rod is 10 cm long. A table is 6 rods long. How long is the table in cm?

10.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
10.link: Ramanujan treated numbers like puzzles to explore, which is what the children do on challenge day.
10.story: Srinivasa Ramanujan was born in Erode, in India. He loved numbers and worked on maths from a young age. He sent his ideas in letters to mathematicians in England, and one of them was G. H. Hardy. Later Ramanujan went to Cambridge to work with him. Hardy told a story that he once rode in taxi number 1729 and called it a dull number. Ramanujan said it was very interesting. Even a plain number can hide a surprise.
10.blurb: Srinivasa Ramanujan (India, 1887-1920) loved numbers and sent his ideas to mathematicians in England. He treated numbers like puzzles to explore.
10.q: Puzzle: find two numbers that add up to 12 and have a difference of 2.
10.legend: Taxi story labelled as 'a story that Hardy told himself'; it is Hardy's own account of the conversation.
